name: Bianca Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58 and a junior developer on parking-permit forms at a tech company, after working at a swimming-pool desk and earning a two-year college diploma. I use AI occasionally to explain an old rule, but a senior checks my changes. Joel, my partner, repairs instruments for schools, our children are grown, and we rent with about four months of expenses saved on a typical developer wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team that a little AI can explain an old parking-permit rule, but someone still has to check the street and date on the permit. I use it occasionally when I am stuck, then compare the answer with the council’s written rule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am 58 and still a junior developer after a two-year college diploma, but this tech-company job pays a typical developer wage. Joel repairs musical instruments at schools, and with our grown children living elsewhere we have about four months of expenses saved and can pay our rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep fixing permit-form bugs and ask the senior developer to review one release with me each Friday. We would keep putting 90 monthly into savings while both wages continue, because the instrument work has school-holiday gaps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel calm about our work and bills in this picture. Four months saved gives us room for a quiet summer when Joel’s school calls slow down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What was a permit bug you fixed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A resident entered a new street number and the form sent the permit to the old address. I checked the saved form against the printed letter before we sent the correction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you use AI for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I sometimes ask it to explain a rule in plain words, but I do not copy its answer into a permit. The council rule, not a fluent paragraph, decides where a car may park.

say: I want **permit dates and streets** checked against written rules.
I use **AI occasionally** to understand rules, then verify them.
think: I have **four months saved** on a typical developer wage.
I see **rent covered** despite Joel’s school-holiday gaps.
do: **Keep fixing permit forms** and ask a senior to review one release with me each Friday.
**Save 90 monthly** while both household wages continue.
S0.quote: The council rule, not a fluent paragraph, decides where a car may park.
fieldNote: Her **occasional AI use** clarifies old rules but never replaces the written permit authority.
The **four-month cushion** covers Joel’s predictable school-holiday gaps without relying on grown children.

steps.text: Keep fixing parking-permit forms with Friday senior review
Save 90 monthly while both household wages continue

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI doing coding, checking and answering residents could swallow the easy permit-form tickets juniors learn on. We should have a worker-group meeting about which staff still checks disputed permits and what notice comes before cuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My paid hours could shrink because I am still learning and the easy bugs are mine. Four months saved and Joel’s wage give us time to react, but a long search would eat that cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d attend the staff association’s meeting this month to ask together for written hours notice. If my manager approves one paid hour a week, I’d learn the new AI permit test on invented addresses and compare it with the written rule; if my hours fall, I’d search paid local software-support vacancies only if their wages cover rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about my own hours, though I could learn with a real test. I would rather find a wrong street in a fake permit than in a resident’s letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the group request?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would ask for the list of permit decisions still assigned to people and the planned junior hours in writing. I would join the group request, not claim to speak alone for everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if paid testing is refused?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my current work and ask for the hours notice. I would not call watching a demonstration the same as learning the tool.

say: I want **group notice** before junior hours fall on the parking-permit team.
I want **resident disputes** checked by a named worker before a permit answer goes out.
think: I could lose **easy permit tickets** and paid hours.
I have **four months saved**, not a year of search money.
do: **Join staff meeting** for written hours notice.
**Learn AI permit tests** weekly only with manager-approved paid time and invented addresses.
**Search paid local support** if hours fall and vacancies cover rent and bills.
S1.quote: I would rather find a wrong street in a fake permit than in a resident’s letter.
fieldNote: She uses a **collective request** for notice rather than assuming her manager will grant it.
The **new AI learning** requires approved paid time and fake addresses, not live resident records.

steps.text: Join staff association meeting to request written junior-hours notice
Practise AI permit tests weekly only with approved paid time and invented addresses
Search paid local software-support vacancies if hours fall and wages cover rent and bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2028 could write the permit code and answer parking questions for less than our team. Robots that place signs or repair instruments may follow around 2031, so our screen work changes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my junior developer role could end quickly; four months saved would give us some search time, but Joel’s school work alone would not pay every bill. I would not promise that a council office is immune to AGI either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the company for written notice and delay replacing our sofa now. If my job ends after 2028, I’d apply for paid local parking-service vacancies only if they exist and wages cover rent and bills; I would ask the public employment office what temporary help we actually qualify for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be alarmed about losing my own wage even with a buffer. Four months is a bridge, not another employer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why parking service if AGI can answer questions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some offices may still need a person for a disputed sign or an appeal, but I do not know which. I would accept only a real paid vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Joel’s instrument work expand?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He could ask schools about more repair days, but they set the budgets. We would not count extra days before a school booked and paid him.

say: I expect **AGI in 2028** to reach permit code before street work.
I expect **physical robots around 2031** to follow later.
think: I expect my **junior wage** could end quickly.
I know **four months saved** buys time, not a replacement salary.
do: **Delay sofa replacement** and request written job-cut notice now.
**Apply for parking service** after 2028 loss only if local vacancies cover rent and bills.
**Ask public employment office** about actual help eligibility if displaced.
S2.quote: Four months is a bridge, not another employer.
fieldNote: She treats **parking-service work** as a possible paid vacancy, not a protected job.
She checks **actual public eligibility** and does not budget for unbooked school repair days.

steps.text: Delay replacing the sofa when developer cuts threaten
Apply for paid local parking-service vacancies if displaced after 2028 and wages cover rent and bills
Ask public employment office about eligibility if displaced

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2031 gives us a few years to test how people appeal a permit error before code changes. Robots for street signs and instrument repairs may arrive around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn to test whether a parking form works for someone who cannot see small text, though AGI may also learn that test. I would need paid time and guidance, and I would keep our four-month reserve intact rather than buying a costly course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the accessibility lead for an approved paid hour each week to practise one screen-reader check on a fake permit form; if she agrees, I’d record the errors and fixes. We would save 70 monthly while both wages hold; after 2031 job loss I’d apply for paid local accessibility-testing vacancies only if I qualify and their wages cover rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about my code role, but more time lets me learn from actual users. A form is not accessible because a developer says it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who checks your work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask a user who relies on a screen reader and the accessibility lead to check a sample form, only with their consent and paid project time. I would not claim one test makes me an expert.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the lead refuses the hour?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep fixing ordinary forms and protect our savings. I would not put a training fee on a credit card to pretend I have a new job.

say: I want **accessible permit forms** tested before AGI reaches code in 2031.
I expect **street robots around 2034** to follow later.
think: I could learn **screen-reader checking** while developer pay lasts.
I need **four months untouched** rather than a costly course.
do: **Practise screen-reader checks** weekly on fake permit forms only with accessibility lead approval, user consent and paid time.
**Apply for testing vacancies** after 2031 job loss only if qualified and paid local openings cover rent and bills.
feel: **Anxious but learning** with an approved real-user check.
S3.quote: A form is not accessible because a developer says it is.
fieldNote: Her **accessibility practice** needs approved paid time and consent from a screen-reader user.
The **testing job route** remains conditional on qualification and bill-covering local vacancies.

steps.text: Practise fake-form screen-reader checks weekly only with lead approval, user consent and paid time
Save 70 monthly while both household wages continue
Apply for paid local accessibility-testing vacancies if displaced after 2031, qualified and wages cover bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say ten years before full AGI in 2036 is enough time to fix bad forms and bargain for notice about any job cuts. Robots doing physical street or instrument work may follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could be nearing the end of paid work, but I have not checked a retirement amount and will not guess at one. If both wages continue, we might build a longer reserve; for now four months saved and a junior title still make me watch the staffing list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep repairing permit forms, attend the association’s annual staffing review and save 80 monthly while both wages continue. I’d request a written retirement-income estimate this year; if my developer job ends after 2036, I’d seek paid local accessibility-testing openings only if I qualify and wages cover rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be uneasy about a later job change but secure in our bills for the next few years. A decade is useful only if we measure what happens during it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put in the review?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for the funded junior hours and how many permit appeals still need people. The association can ask together; a promise in a hallway is easy to forget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your grown children help you stop work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I love them, but they have their own households. Joel and I will use our wages and a verified retirement figure, not their pay, for the plan.

say: I want **annual staffing figures** before AGI reaches permit code in 2036.
I expect **street robots around 2039** to follow later.
think: I cannot assume **retirement income** without a written estimate.
I might build **more reserve** only if both wages continue.
do: **Keep fixing forms** and join annual association staffing review.
**Save 80 monthly** while both wages hold; request written retirement-income estimate.
**Seek paid testing vacancies** after 2036 displacement only if qualified local openings cover rent and bills.
feel: **Uneasy later**, financially secure in the next few years.
S4.quote: A decade is useful only if we measure what happens during it.
fieldNote: Her **current four-month cushion** supports near-term stability while job change remains uncertain.
The **annual group review** and written income estimate provide facts without assuming a pension or child support.

Save 80 monthly while both wages hold and request written retirement-income estimate

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because it could end my junior wage before a bill-covering local opening appears. Written notice, a real paid parking-service vacancy and verified temporary public support would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether school-holiday repair gaps make Joel’s wage useless. We plan for school-holiday gaps, but we cannot turn an unbooked repair day into income.

headlineQuote: We plan for school-holiday gaps, but we cannot turn an unbooked repair day into income.
portrait: Bianca is a **58-year-old junior developer** with a two-year diploma, typical pay and four months saved.
She and Joel **rent** while his school instrument repairs vary across holidays.
She **uses AI occasionally** and favours group staffing notice and approved paid learning.
Her **2028 worry** is a lost developer wage before a paid parking-service job appears.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her junior wage before a bill-covering vacancy appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, a paid parking-service opening and verified public support would help.
